frase_gancho.texto: A European violin that the sierra learned to play in its own way.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the sierra we descend to the desert coast. Look for a large plate woven in a spiral, with reddish-brown geometric designs.

guion_corto.texto: This violin and this drum are the sacred instruments of the Rarámuri, or Tarahumara, the people of the Sierra Madre Occidental, in Chihuahua. The violin arrived with the Jesuit missionaries in the seventeenth century, but the Rarámuri did not copy it: they made it their own. They carve it by hand from pine wood with simple tools, and its sound is rough and sweet at the same time. Beside it is a drum with two goatskin heads, held in place with leather straps. Together they accompany the dances of the festivals, such as the yúmari. For the Rarámuri, playing and dancing are not entertainment: they are a prayer with the body, which delights Onorúame, their god, and helps keep the world in balance.

guion_largo.texto:
Rarámuri means “those of the light feet.” The name Tarahumara is a Spanish adaptation. They live in one of the most rugged regions of the country, the Sierra Madre Occidental, where the Copper Canyon is found, a system of canyons that some compare to the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. The name is said to come from the greenish color of its walls. Here is a detail that may sound familiar: in the halls downstairs you saw copper bells, which traveled as far as the desert of Paquimé.

The first thing people say about them is that they are great runners. In the rarajípari, two teams kick a wooden ball across the sierra for hours, and the race can cover more than a hundred kilometers. The women have their own race, with a hoop and a stick. Running is a way of being together and of moving through a territory made of ravines, and that is where the name comes from.

The violin is the instrument of the festivals. The curious thing is that it did not belong to this world: it arrived with the Jesuits, along with guitars and European religious singing. The Rarámuri transformed it. Each musician makes his own with a knife and wood from the sierra, and plays it in his own style. It is the same instrument you saw in the Huasteca, where it leads the huapango, and in the dance of the Negritos: a European violin that, over the centuries, became the instrument of many Indigenous peoples.

The yúmari is a ceremony of songs and dance to ask for rain, health and a good harvest. It is danced in the courtyard, in a circle, with small steps that follow the rhythm of the violin and the drum, and it can last all night. The belief is powerful: if the Rarámuri stopped playing and dancing, the balance of the world would break, and according to some accounts even the Sun would go out.

Onorúame, whose name is usually translated as God the Father, has a companion, Eyerúame, the Mother. Together they look after the world, and the people return the favor with music, dance and food. It is a beautiful idea of reciprocity: you receive, you give thanks, and you give something in return. Music is the way of saying thank you.

Look closely at the drum. It has two skin heads, tightened with leather cords to adjust them to the climate of the canyon. At the festivals, moreover, tesgüino is passed around, a fermented maize drink shared at community work gatherings and at celebrations. Behind the music, then, there is also the cornfield, that thread you already saw running across the whole Upper Floor.

The Rarámuri also have their own Holy Week, with Pharisees and ceremonies of their own, though different from those of the Yaqui. And in this very hall there is a mural by the painter Pablo O’Higgins dedicated to the sierra, which you can look at after this instrument to imagine the landscape where it sounds.

A borrowed violin, a god of their own, a music that sustains the world. What the Rarámuri did with this instrument is what the Yaqui did with Holy Week: take something that came from outside and make it part of their way of life.

texto: Look for the hand-carved violin and the curved bow
Observe the skin heads of the drum and the cords that hold them
Imagine the sound of the yúmari playing all night long

texto.Technique/Material: Hand-carved pine/ash wood, goatskin and plant-based glues
texto.Function: Liturgical musical instruments for ceremonial dances (matachines and yumari)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The violin is foreign to Indigenous peoples.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It arrived with the Jesuits, but the Rarámuri made it their own: they build it, play it and use it in their ceremonies.
